reviews.summary: The one reviewer found the exam in line with the tutorials and the content more intuitive than it first looks.

notes.coursework: One written coursework (20%); unassessed tutorial exercises, about half discussed in class.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, all 3 questions, open book, all proof: NP-completeness and logspace reductions, NL, NC and oracle classes.
notes.examiners: 2024-25: marks lost for non-total reductions and malformed clauses.
notes.caveat: Each question needs a fresh reduction idea, so open book helps less than it seems; mean about 65.

reviews.summary: Reviewers found the content interesting and the tutorials manageable, but all four found the exam much harder and longer than the course prepared them for.

notes.coursework: Assessed exercises plus implementing and testing a portfolio optimisation model (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, all 3 questions, calculator: ~45% derivations (portfolios, CAPM), ~40% calculations (binomial option pricing).
notes.examiners: No recent report: the last paper was for resit students only; last mean 69.8 (2023-24).
notes.caveat: Reviewers found the exam much harder and longer than the tutorials suggested.

reviews.summary: Reviewers split: one found the exam as expected thanks to plenty of practice papers, the other wanted more depth on the maths and found the exam very hard.

notes.coursework: Assessed exercises (30%), the Kryptonite-N project; not difficult but time-consuming.
notes.exam: 70%: 90 min, 2 questions of 50% each, closed book, no calculator: mostly textbook derivations (MLE, estimator bias, conjugate priors).
notes.examiners: No report since 2022-23.
notes.caveat: With only two questions, one blank derivation costs a lot.

reviews.summary: Reviewers rated it highly: clear teaching, current content and easy coursework, though fast-paced with a lot to cover.

notes.coursework: Implement and test smart contracts in Foundry (in 2023 an NFT ticketing contract plus an ERC20 token), 20%; this year's not out yet.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, both questions: short concept answers plus an AMM calculation, then find the bug in a ~40-line Solidity contract.
notes.examiners: Dec 2025: a slightly harder paper than in earlier years; examiners want concise answers.
notes.caveat: Fast-paced with a lot of content; examiners advise attending the lectures.

reviews.summary: Reviewers praised the teaching and found the exam fair, but the material hard and unusual, needing a lot of practice.

notes.coursework: Two assessed coursework tests (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, all 3 questions, no calculator: ~75% Dirac-notation calculation (teleportation, QFT, Grover, error-correcting codes).
notes.examiners: 2024-25: generally went well; the complexity comparison and Q3c were the hardest parts.
notes.caveat: Means were about 66 in both recent years; plan on a lot of practice with the exercises.

reviews.summary: Reviewers liked the papers and case studies and found the coursework easy, but said the slides alone weren't enough and much had to be learned from the papers.

notes.coursework: Two one-page worksheets (20%) that reviewers found very easy.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, one question per lecturer: explain 15-20 systems (Spanner, Dynamo, Bigtable...) and apply them to a scenario; no maths.
notes.examiners: Dec 2025 report unavailable; in 2024-25 vague or off-target answers lost marks.
notes.caveat: Expect a lot of self-study from the research papers; reviewers found the slides thin on their own.

notes.coursework: Two coursework exercises (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, both questions, all separation-logic proof: assertions and proof sketches for list and tree algorithms.
notes.examiners: No report since 2022-23.
notes.caveat: All formal proof: formulaic but long and notation-heavy, so small slips cost marks.

reviews.summary: The one reviewer rated the teaching highly and found the module valuable, but the courseworks and exam demanding and some tools niche.

notes.coursework: Team project in groups of 2-3 (30%): study a reliability tool from its paper, extend its evaluation, then report and present.
notes.exam: 70%: 90 min, two compulsory questions on code and tool internals (ASan, KLEE, AFL); guest lectures are examinable.
notes.examiners: 2024-25 (MEng paper): all did well; slips on ASan redzones and KLEE path details.
notes.caveat: Teams and project choice are due 13 Oct; the last MSc mean (61.4) is the lowest in autumn.

reviews.summary: Reviewers valued the guest speakers and having no exam, but found the weekly group deliverables time-consuming and wanted clearer marking criteria and faster feedback.

notes.coursework: A 2% individual declaration, then in groups of 3: weekly worksheets 33%, presentation 25% (6 Nov), final report 40% (27 Nov).
notes.caveat: Not recorded (by design) and Thursday attendance is expected; reviewers say top marks on the weekly deliverables are hard to get.

coursework.title: MDP, DP, MC, TD, Value-function Approx, Policy Gradients

reviews.summary: All three reviewers praised the clear, well-prepared teaching; one noted the module was restructured in 2025-26.

notes.coursework: One individual theory-and-code piece (30%), out 3 Nov, due 17 Nov, about 4 h; weekly tutorials are ungraded.
notes.exam: 70%: worked by hand: a grid-world MDP, policy evaluation and value iteration, then MC, TD, SARSA and Q-learning step by step.
notes.examiners: Dec 2025: strong overall, Q2 and Q3 harder than Q1; formulas without the numbers lost marks.
notes.caveat: The Friday lab isn't recorded; the 66.0 mean is from 2024-25, before the restructure.

reviews.summary: Reviewers found it well organised, with time-consuming group courseworks and a tight exam; one found it repetitive after earlier ML courses.

notes.coursework: Two group courseworks in groups of 4 (Python/NumPy): decision trees (12%) and a neural-network library plus regressor (18%).
notes.exam: 70%: 90 min, 3 questions, one A4 notes sheet: ~90% calculation (information gain, k-means/GMM, backprop); tight on time.
notes.examiners: Dec 2025: Q1a was answered well by most; marks lost to occasional calculation slips.
notes.caveat: New lead lecturer this year; largely a repeat if you have already taken an ML course.

reviews.summary: One reviewer found the workload high, with many algorithms and proofs to memorise; the other found it straightforward, preferred the game-theory part and enjoyed the coursework.

notes.coursework: One group coursework (20%), e.g. a branch-and-bound scheduler plus report; out 2 Nov, due 18 Nov, about 15 h.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 2 questions, closed book: ~70% algorithms by hand (scheduling, Nash equilibria, auctions), ~15% proofs, ~15% reasoning.
notes.examiners: Dec 2025: step-by-step proofs beat qualitative arguments; calculation slips cost marks.
notes.caveat: Last year's exam had an unseen proof; the tutorial sheets include exam-style problems.

notes.coursework: 100% coursework: a 20-30 page report on a self-chosen advanced topic plus an oral presentation, each passed separately.
notes.caveat: Needs a willing supervisor before choices close on 23 Oct; effectively a spring module.

reviews.summary: Reviewers rated the teaching very highly and liked the flipped format and article-based exam, while warning there is a lot of content.

notes.coursework: Two pieces (20%): a simulator lab finding the lowest-energy configuration, then an open-ended piece in groups of up to 3.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, open book, 3 open-ended questions mostly on a recent processor article handed out in advance; no maths.
notes.examiners: Dec 2025 paper built on AMD's Zen 5 guide; in 2024-25 any well-argued answer earned credit.
notes.caveat: Heavy: lots of content, time-consuming coursework, and Monday's material is watched at home.

reviews.summary: The one reviewer found the content interesting and the teaching good, and the 2025-26 exam harder than in previous years.

notes.coursework: Labs (Thu and Fri), 20%.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, all 3 questions: mostly concepts and sketches (neuron models, networks) plus ODE and mutual-information calculations.
notes.examiners: 2024-25: Q1 hardest, Q2 best answered; marks lost for missing proofs, mixed-up plots and units.

notes.coursework: 30%: two in-class exercises, a short programming assignment and a group project with peer evaluation.
notes.exam: 70%: 2 h, 3 questions (2023-24): user-study design writing, Markov-chain calculations and multi-select MCQs.
notes.examiners: 2023-24: most did well; marks lost for study designs lacking controls and HMM vs POMDP mix-ups.
notes.caveat: Didn't run in 2024-25 or 2025-26, so the only paper and feedback are from 2023-24.

reviews.summary: The one reviewer found the content interesting and useful, the coursework simple and the exam balanced, though some proofs take time.

notes.coursework: 20%; in 2023 it was a mid-term in-class paper test.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, both questions: MacKay-style calculations (entropy, KL, Hamming codes), definitions and some derivations.
notes.examiners: 2024-25: some parts built to stretch; slips on normalisation, decodability and the Gaussian LLR.
notes.caveat: The mean fell from 76.3 to 66.9 in 2024-25, and some proofs take time.

reviews.summary: Reviewers praised the teaching and the consistent exam style but found the content large and fast-paced; the coursework was manageable.

notes.coursework: Two Jupyter-notebook courseworks (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, all 3 questions: ~40% calculation (Sobel, camera projection, epipolar lines), ~40% outlining methods.
notes.examiners: 2024-25: partial credit needed correct working; procedural slips and the epipolar proof cost the most.
notes.caveat: A lot of fast-paced content; mean 66.5 in 2024-25.

notes.coursework: One individual coursework (20%): an image generator (VAEs) scored on metrics; out 22 Oct, due 20 Nov, about 16 h.
notes.exam: 80%: 3 questions of 20 marks: about half conceptual, a quarter calculation, a quarter derivation (ELBO, Gaussian KL, diffusion).
notes.examiners: Spring 2026: high raw exam marks; Q2 (receptive field, attention, LoRA rank) separated the class.
notes.caveat: Page says weekly videos plus a class, but CELCAT books two lectures; same course as spring 70010.

reviews.summary: Split: one found the lecturer very helpful and the examinable material clear, the other found the first run still taking shape; both found the CUDA coursework hard without prior experience.

notes.coursework: An individual assignment implementing and optimising ML operators in CUDA, code plus report (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 questions of 3 parts, ~70% calculation (roofline, compression ratios, tiling, KV-cache memory).
notes.examiners: 2025-26: Q1 answered well; Q2 errors on compression metadata, per-tile latency and KV blocks.
notes.caveat: Only one previous run: no past papers, just a mock exam.

notes.coursework: One piece mixing theory and practice (20%).
notes.exam: 80% written exam; no MSc past paper, since it ran as MEng COMP60023.
notes.caveat: Shares its exam slot and Tue/Thu slots with Scheduling and Comp. Finance.

notes.coursework: Two courseworks, alone or in pairs: HDR and image-based lighting, then Monte Carlo rendering (30%).
notes.exam: 70%: 90 min, 2 questions, about 60% numeric calculation (radiometry, HDR, sampling) and 40% short concepts.
notes.examiners: Students did well overall, Q2 a little less so; slips on light fields, Fresnel and sampling.
notes.caveat: About 26 sub-parts in 90 min, with many formulas to memorise and no formula sheet.

notes.coursework: Three individual paper summaries (10%) and a group Android malvertising assignment run as a competition (10%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, all 4 questions: scenario reasoning, MCQs needing a justification, and writing an SELinux policy.
notes.examiners: MCQs went well; unjustified answers and SELinux syntax errors lost marks.
notes.caveat: One half is built on new real-world incidents each year, so it can't be memorised.

notes.coursework: Two courseworks (20%), essentially two past exam questions.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, answer both: about 80% short show/justify derivations on toy functions (convexity, KKT, descent methods).
notes.examiners: Most students did very well; marks lost for unjustified claims and half-answers.
notes.caveat: Marks need full justification; Misener now teaches alone, so the old split may change.

notes.coursework: One term-long project to design, build and evaluate a deep generative model for images (20%).
notes.exam: 80%; the last Deep Learning paper: 90 min, 2 questions, 1-page sheet, MCQs, calculations, derivations and design.
notes.examiners: Deep Learning 2024-25: the conditional GAN question was the hardest; examiners found the paper long.
notes.caveat: Rebuilt from Deep Learning, so old papers only partly apply; same syllabus as 70113, take one.

notes.coursework: One mini-project in groups of two (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 2 questions: hand calculation (convolutions), short recall, MCQs and pseudo-code tied to the tutorials.
notes.examiners: Mostly good; errors on transposed convolutions, U-Nets and unjustified causal claims.
notes.caveat: Strong medical-imaging focus; one older review found much overlap with Computer Vision.

notes.coursework: One coursework on a real NLP shared task (30%); a past one detected patronising language with BERT.
notes.exam: 70%: 90 min, 3 compulsory questions: 2-3 sentence answers plus calculations (word2vec, perplexity, BPE, attention).
notes.examiners: Examiners note marks may be scaled toward the department's 60-70 target.
notes.caveat: New lead lecturer this year, and it shares an exam slot with Networked Systems.

notes.coursework: One coursework, partly programming (20%).
notes.exam: 80%; the 2023 paper: 2 h, 3 questions, closed book with a formula sheet (graphical models, VI, decision theory).
notes.examiners: 2022-23: reasonable overall; the variational inference question was the hardest.
notes.caveat: New team and only one old paper from a previous lecturer; maths heavy.

notes.coursework: Two in-class tests (20%), which can't be AI-assisted.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 3 questions, closed book: about 75% mechanical analyses (reaching definitions, 0-CFA), 20% formal definitions.
notes.examiners: A standard paper and most did well; abstract interpretation and matrix sizes cost marks.
notes.caveat: Dense formal notation, and it shares an exam slot with spring Generative AI.

notes.coursework: Two written pieces of 10% each, which may be done in pairs.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 3 questions on one game model: run CTL/ATL model checking, plus small proofs and counterexamples.
notes.examiners: Mostly correct; marks lost for too little detail and missing counterexamples.
notes.caveat: Renamed from Modal Logic; the new safe-AI and RL material has no past paper.

notes.coursework: Two individual pieces of 15% each; the second is a simulated-robot strategy ending in a live competition.
notes.exam: 70%: 90 min, 3 questions, open book: mostly short reasoning plus some modelling and derivation.
notes.examiners: Q2 answered best and Q3 the hardest; vague answers and copied slide phrases lost marks.
notes.caveat: Assumes autumn Reinforcement Learning or equivalent; each question ends with an unusual part.

notes.coursework: One individual coursework of about 10 h with essay, numerical and tool-based parts (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 2 questions: circuits in Ruby notation, then MaxJ dataflow code and design.
notes.examiners: Most had no major problems; slips in wiring, MaxJ types and PCIe bandwidth.
notes.caveat: A large part of the first half is learning Ruby, a niche hardware notation.

notes.coursework: Two courseworks, often in pairs: profiling, micro-benchmarks and thread-safe C++ (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 2 questions: applied analysis (lock-free code, profiles, counters), essay-like explanation, some calculation.
notes.examiners: Only Q1 feedback published: it went well overall; errors on races and bottleneck terms.
notes.caveat: Low mean (62.7), only two past papers, and heavy use of C++.

notes.coursework: One interpretability lab: run explainability tools on a model and write a technical report (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: mostly causality (structural causal models, do-calculus, identifiability, counterfactuals).
notes.caveat: Rebuilt from an ethics module, so there is no past paper or mean.

notes.coursework: One individual coursework, a short test-like analysis (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h in the labs, 2 questions, one A4 sheet: about half live hacking on VMs, half written.
notes.examiners: Generic written answers lost marks; the later flags and the session forgery were the hardest.
notes.caveat: Mean 60.8 in 2024-25; the practical half rewards regular CTF practice.

notes.coursework: Three individual shader tasks (20%): illumination 40%, texture 10%, GPU ray tracer 50%.
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 2 questions: a design essay with some maths, MCQs and calculation.
notes.examiners: Q1 only: MCQs went well, stricter thresholds applied; matrix questions now dropped.
notes.caveat: New co-lecturer and a shift toward 3D vision, so past papers predict less.

notes.coursework: Two pieces of 10% each.
notes.exam: 80%: 3 questions (per 2025-26 feedback): ILP derivations, completeness and consistency proofs, probabilistic BDDs.
notes.examiners: Marks lost for skipping steps and not using the method the question asked for.
notes.caveat: No past paper or mean, and it assumes basic logic and Prolog.

notes.coursework: One written coursework (20%).
notes.exam: 80%: 2 h, 3 questions, almost all guided multi-part proofs (circuit, monotone and resolution lower bounds).
notes.examiners: Handled reasonably well; marks lost in intermediate justifications.
notes.caveat: Proof-heavy exam built on lower-bound techniques few students have seen before.

modules.title: Software Engineering for Machine Learning Systems

notes.coursework: About 6 pieces: one individual Docker predictor, then group design, service, Kubernetes, monitoring and a 2-week live run.
notes.caveat: The final live run is marked on meeting service targets and depends on your group.

notes.coursework: One coursework 30%, a team project (up to 5 people) 40%, and weekly timed quizzes 30%.
notes.caveat: The weekly timed quizzes force steady study all term.

reviews.summary: Reviewers rated the teaching very highly, but found the weekly research paper to read and discuss, plus intense coursework, demanding.

notes.coursework: Three small courseworks building a middlebox in eBPF, DPDK or P4 (30%).
notes.exam: 70%: 90 min, 2 questions: half recall of class topics, half continuing an in-class design exercise.
notes.examiners: Students did well overall; generic answers not tied to the class design scored low.
notes.caveat: Assumes networking background, and it shares an exam slot with NLP.

notes.coursework: Several theory and coding exercises (30%).
notes.exam: 70%: 2 h, 2 long guided questions: differential-geometry derivations, algorithms and discussion.
notes.caveat: New maths (Riemannian geometry), one past paper and a low mean of 63.4.

notes.coursework: Two assignments covering theory and coding (30%).
notes.exam: 70%, described only as testing conceptual understanding; new module, no past paper.
notes.caveat: First run with a new lecturer, so there is no past paper or mean.

modules.title: Generative Methods in AI for Science

notes.coursework: Four bi-weekly open-ended research sprints in groups of 1-3 (20%).
notes.exam: A traditional exam (80%); new module, no past paper.
notes.caveat: Very maths heavy: expects Deep Learning and Maths for ML, plus weekly paper reading.
